The Problem With Pure --sref For This Job

--sref transfers aesthetic (color, texture, brushwork) but does NOT preserve composition or structure. Style Reference captures the overall mood, including colors, textures, lighting, and medium — it doesn't copy the actual objects or subjects. So if you just throw your hallway in as a reference and your two character portraits as --sref, Midjourney will give you a hallway in that art style but the lockers, runes, vines, door layout, floor pattern — none of that geometry is guaranteed to come back.

To preserve structure of the hallway while transferring style from the portraits, you need to use the hallway itself as an image prompt (not --sref), and the portraits as --sref. Image prompts in MJ V7 influence composition and content; sref influences aesthetic. That's the split you need.

The Nano Banana Pro Prompt — Add Powered-Up Character To Dark Hallway

Setup:

Image 1: The dark hallway environment (FlashBoards_Creative_AI_Canvas__66_.png) → composition source

Image 2: The character portrait (Young_Man_Portrait_from_Midjourney.png) → character identity source

Prompt:

Reference image 1: this is the COMPOSITION AND ENVIRONMENT SOURCE. 
Preserve its exact framing, camera angle, perspective, lighting, color 
palette, atmosphere, art style, and every architectural element — the 
stone brick walls, the row of dark metal lockers on the left, the 
glowing magical vines spilling from the ceiling, the small floating 
purple and cyan light orbs, the runes and chalk symbols on the right 
wall, the cracked stone floor tiles, and the wooden door at the far 
end. Nothing in the environment should change. Match its art style 
exactly across the entire output.

Reference image 2: this is the CHARACTER IDENTITY SOURCE. Preserve the 
character's exact face, beard, glasses, black Nike cap, hair, skin 
tone, and orange Nike sweatshirt with the dark horizontal chest stripe. 
Keep him recognizably the same person.

Place this character into the scene from image 1, standing on the right 
side of the frame in the foreground, three-quarter body visible from 
the waist up, body angled slightly toward the camera, facing forward 
looking toward the viewer. He is in a POWERED-UP STATE: visibly bulked 
and muscular, his shoulders broader, chest expanded, biceps and forearms 
swollen with energy, the orange Nike sweatshirt stretched tight across 
his enlarged chest and arms with small tears at the seams of the 
shoulders and along the sleeve where the fabric has split from the 
muscle expansion. His expression is intense, charged, fierce — eyes 
locked forward, jaw set, breathing hard from the surge of power. Faint 
cyan and magenta energy still radiating subtly from his skin and edges, 
catching the rim of his silhouette.

Light him with the existing scene lighting from image 1 — cool deep 
purples and cyans across the body, soft magenta rim highlights from 
the wall orbs behind him, his face partially lit from the cyan glow of 
the vines above. He should look fully embedded in the environment, not 
pasted on. Match the painted illustration style of image 1 across the 
character — same brushwork, same outline treatment, same color grading, 
same rendering quality. He must look like he was always part of the 
same artwork.

Aspect ratio: match image 1 (16:9 widescreen).

Why Each Block Matters

Environment lockdown — listing every element by name forces NBP to preserve the lockers, vines, runes, door rather than reinterpret them

Character identity lockdown — explicit description of clothing/face anchors identity; the portrait reference alone isn't enough

Position spec — "right side, three-quarter body, waist up, facing forward" gives NBP exactly where to place him so he matches your mental composition

Bulk-up direction — describes the muscular state in physical terms (which muscles, where the fabric tears) so it reads as a "powered-up version of the same guy" not a different character

Lighting integration — calling out the actual light sources from image 1 (cyan vines, magenta orbs) makes the character look lit BY the scene rather than lit separately and dropped in

Style match directive — last paragraph forces the character to be rendered in the environment's painted style, not the cleaner inked style from his portrait

If The First Generation Drifts

Common drifts and the fix message:

If he looks pasted on / different art style than the hallway:

Keep everything the same but blend the character more into the painted 
style of image 1. He currently looks like he was rendered in a different 
style than the environment. Match the brushwork, outline treatment, and 
color grading of image 1 exactly across his entire body, clothing, and 
face. He should look like he was painted into the scene by the same 
artist, not added on top.

If the bulk is too cartoonish / Hulk-like:

Keep everything the same but tone down the muscle expansion. Make him 
look like a normal guy who has just gotten visibly stronger and pumped 
— broader shoulders, fuller arms, tight sweatshirt — not like a 
bodybuilder or comic book hulk. Realistic athletic bulk, not exaggerated.

If position is wrong:

Keep everything the same but move the character. He should be on the 
right side of the frame, three-quarter body framing from the waist up, 
facing the camera directly. Right now he is [describe what's wrong].

One Recommendation Before You Generate

Before locking this last frame, decide one thing: does the camera also push in or pull back during the transition? If yes, the framing of your last frame should already reflect the end-of-camera-move position, not match image 1's framing. If the camera holds static throughout the bulk-up, then matching image 1's framing exactly is correct.

For Seedance to interpolate cleanly, first frame and last frame need to share the same camera position OR have a clean intentional camera move between them. Mismatched framing with no clear move = jittery output.

One important warning before the prompt: First/last frame pinning works best when the last frame already contains the character in his end position. You're asking Seedance to interpolate a character INTO the last frame from nothing, which is harder. There are two ways to handle this:

Option A (cleaner, recommended): Use Nano Banana Pro first to drop the powered-up character into the dark hallway (the prompt I gave you in the previous message), then use THAT as the last frame. Seedance interpolates only motion + lighting between two complete frames. This produces dramatically better results.

Option B (one-shot, riskier): Feed Seedance the bare dark hallway as last frame + character portrait as reference, and pray it places him correctly. Seedance will sometimes nail it, sometimes spawn him in the wrong spot or lose him entirely.

I'll write the prompt for Option B since you asked for it, but prepare for 2–3 generations to land it. Option A is one Nano Banana call + one Seedance call, basically the same effort with much higher hit rate.

frame. <<<image_3>>> is the character identity reference — preserve 
his face, beard, glasses, black Nike cap, and orange Nike sweatshirt 
across the entire shot. The video must start matching image 1 perfectly 
and end matching image 2 perfectly, with the character present on the 
right side of the final frame in his powered-up state.

[0:00–0:02] Hold opens on the bright purple hallway. The character 
stands on the right side of frame, body angled toward camera, 
breathing hard after the kill. Camera holds locked-off, no movement. 
Vines glow soft cyan and pink overhead, magenta orbs steady on the 
walls. Low ambient hum of magical energy, the character's heavy breath.

[0:02–0:06] Energy surges through the character. His shoulders broaden, 
chest expands, arms swell with muscle, the orange Nike sweatshirt 
stretches tight across his torso, fabric tearing along the shoulder 
seams and sleeve edges. Faint cyan and magenta energy radiates from 
his skin, rim-lighting his silhouette. His jaw clenches, eyes lock 
forward, breath turns to a low growl. Camera holds steady. Sound: 
deep low-frequency rumble building, fabric ripping, sharp breath, 
energy crackle.

[0:06–0:09] The hallway lights flicker violently. Magenta orbs pulse 
and stutter, vine glow surges and dims, ambient light strobes between 
bright purple and near-black. Each flicker holds dimmer than the last. 
Character stays locked in his powered-up stance, energy still radiating 
but cooling. Camera holds steady. Sound: electrical buzz-out, glass 
hum, pulses of low bass with each flicker, then silence between.

[0:09–0:12] Lights stabilize at their darkest setting. The hallway is 
now deep blue-black with only the cyan vine glow and dim magenta orbs 
remaining. Character holds his pumped stance on the right side of 
frame, rim-lit by the surviving cyan light, chest rising and falling. 
Final frame matches image 2 exactly, with the character composited on 
the right. Sound: low magical hum, slow heavy breathing, stillness.

Camera: locked-off static medium shot throughout. No pan, no zoom, no 
push. The transition is in lighting and character state, not camera.

Style: preserve the painted illustration style of image 1 and image 2 
across every frame.

[Duration: 12s | Ratio: 16:9 | Resolution: 1080p | Audio: on]

Key Choices In This Prompt

Locked-off camera — any camera move would fight the bulk-up + lighting transition. Save camera moves for shots where they're the point.

Three distinct beats — bulk-up first (0:02–0:06), then flicker (0:06–0:09), then dark settle (0:09–0:12). Trying to overlap them confuses Seedance.

"Each flicker holds dimmer than the last" — gives Seedance a directional cue for the lighting curve instead of random strobing.

Sound design per beat — Seedance generates audio in the same pass; specific sound cues per phase make the audio feel intentional.

12 seconds total — within the 4–15s limit, gives each beat ~3 seconds which is the minimum for a state change to read on screen.

The reason is that Seedance places characters poorly when there's no anchor in the last frame — you lose 1–2 generations to mis-placed character before getting it right, and each Seedance generation costs more credits than one NBP call.
